L7: # Authorize service principal access to Databricks with OAuth
L8: 
L9: This page explains how to authorize access to Databricks resources from unattended processes, such as automated CLI commands or REST API calls made from scripts or applications.
L10: Databricks uses cite2†OAuth 2.0†auth0.com as the preferred protocol for service principal authorization and authentication outside of the UI. Unified client authentication automates token generation and refresh. When a service principal signs in and is granted consent, OAuth issues an access token for the CLI, SDK, or other tool to use on its behalf. Each access token is valid for one hour, after which a new token is automatically requested.
L11: In this page, authorization refers to using OAuth to grant a service principal access to Databricks resources, while authentication refers to validating credentials through access tokens.
L12: 
L13: For more high-level details, see cite3†Authorize access to Databricks resources .
L14: ## Ways to authorize a service principalcite4†​ L15: 
L16: Databricks supports the following ways to authorize a service principal:
L17: 
L18:   * Automatic (recommended): Use cite5†unified authentication with supported tools and SDKs, such as the Databricks Terraform SDK. This approach handles token generation and refresh automatically, and is ideal for automation or other unattended workloads.
L19:   * Manual: Generate a code verifier and challenge, then exchange them for an OAuth token. Use this method if your tool or API doesn’t support unified authentication. You may need to build your own token refresh mechanism for your application. For details, see cite6†Manually generate OAuth M2M access tokens .
L20:   * OAuth OBO: Act as a service principal you manage through the standard user (U2M) OAuth flow, without an OAuth secret. Use this for interactive access when a person drives the session. See cite7†Authenticate as a service principal using OAuth OBO .
L21: ## Prerequisitescite8†​ L22: 
L23: Before you configure OAuth, perform the following steps:
L24: 
L25:   1. Create a Databricks service principal. See cite9†Add service principals to your account .
L26:   2. Go to the Configuration tab for the service principal and select the entitlements it should have for this workspace.
L27:   3. Go to the Permissions tab and grant access to any Databricks users, service principals, and groups that you want to manage and use this service principal. See cite10†Who can manage and use service principals? .
L28: ## Authenticate as a service principal using OAuth OBOcite11†​ L29: 
L30: Beta
L31: 
L32: This feature is in cite12†Beta .
L33: 
L34: OAuth on-behalf-of (OBO) lets you obtain a token that acts with a service principal's identity instead of your own user account, using the standard U2M OAuth flow.
L35: 
L36: You must have the Service Principal Manager role on the service principal that you want to authenticate as. If you created the service principal, you have this role automatically. See cite13†Roles for managing service principals .
L37:   1. Initiate the standard U2M flow. The following example uses the Databricks CLI:
L38: 
L39:     `databricks auth login --host <workspace-url>
L40:     `
L41: 
L42:   2. A browser window opens for authorization. From the dropdown, select the service principal to authenticate as, then authorize the application.
L43:   3. The OAuth token is issued with the service principal's identity. The `sub` claim in the token corresponds to the selected service principal. To view the token, run:
L44: 
L45:     `databricks auth token --host <workspace-url>
L46:     `
L47: 
L48: This flow works with any application that supports standard U2M authentication. For the complete steps, see cite14†Automatic authorization with unified authentication or cite15†Manually generate OAuth U2M access tokens .
L49: ## Authorize with OAuth M2M using a client ID and secretcite16†​ L50: 
L51: For unattended workloads such as automation, scripts, and CI/CD, create an OAuth secret for the service principal and exchange it for short-lived access tokens using the client credentials (M2M) flow.
L52: ### Step 1: Create an OAuth secretcite17†​ L53: 
L54: To authorize access to your Databricks resources with OAuth, you must create an OAuth secret. The secret is used to generate OAuth access tokens for authentication. A service principal can have up to five OAuth secrets, and each secret can be valid for up to two years.
L55: 
L56: Account admins and workspace admins can create an OAuth secret for a service principal.
L57:   1. Click your username in the top bar and select Settings.
L58:   2. Click the Identity and access tab.
L59:   3. Next to Service principals, click Manage.
L60:   4. Select the service principal.
L61:   5. Click the Secrets tab.
L62:   6. Click Generate secret.
L63:   7. Set the secret’s lifetime in days (maximum 730 days).
L64:   8. Under Scopes, select the API scopes the secret can use. To restrict the secret, search for and select one or more scopes, such as `sql` or `jobs`. To let the secret access every API the service principal is authorized for, select all APIs (not recommended). See cite18†Scoped OAuth secrets .
L65:   9. Click Generate.
L66:   10. Copy the displayed secret and client ID, then click Done. The secret is shown only once. The client ID is the same as the service principal’s application ID.
L67: Account admins can also create an OAuth secret from the account console. From the User management tab, select the service principal, then go to the Credentials & secrets tab.
L68: 
L69: note
L70: 
L71: To enable the service principal to use clusters or SQL warehouses, you must give the service principal access to them. See cite19†Compute permissions or cite20†Manage a SQL warehouse .
L72: #### Scoped OAuth secretscite21†​ L73: 
L74: By default, an OAuth secret can access every API the service principal is authorized for (`all-apis`). A scoped secret restricts access to a specific set of API scopes, such as `sql`, `jobs`, or `unity-catalog`. An OAuth access token minted from a scoped secret can't exceed the secret’s scopes, which limits the impact if the secret is leaked or misused. Databricks recommends binding each secret to only the scopes its integration needs.
L75: A secret created without scopes, including every existing secret, keeps `all-apis` access and behaves as before.
L76: 
L77: Scopes are set when you generate the secret and can’t be changed afterward. To use different scopes, generate a new secret. In the Secrets table, click Clone on an existing secret to create a new one with the same scopes and lifetime.
L78: 
L79: warning
L80: 
L81: A secret with the `authentication` scope can create new tokens with any scope. Bind this scope only to secrets that manage other credentials.
L82: For the full list of scopes and the API operations each one covers, see cite22†API scopes .
L83: ### Step 2: Use OAuth authorizationcite23†​ L84: 
L85: To use OAuth authorization with the unified authentication tool, you must set the following associated environment variables, `.databrickscfg` fields, Terraform fields, or `Config` fields:
L86:   * The Databricks host, specified as `https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com` for account operations or the target cite24†workspace URL , for example `https://dbc-a1b2345c-d6e7.cloud.databricks.com` for workspace operations.
L87:   * The Databricks account ID, for Databricks account operations.
L88:   * The service principal client ID.
L89:   * The service principal secret.
L90: 
L91: To perform OAuth service principal authentication, integrate the following within your code, based on the participating tool or SDK:
L92:   * Environment
L93:   * Profile
L94:   * CLI
L95:   * Connect
L96:   * VS Code
L97:   * Terraform
L98:   * Python
L99:   * Java
L100:   * Go
L101: 
L102: To use environment variables for a specific Databricks authentication type with a tool or SDK, see cite3†Authorize access to Databricks resources or the tool's or SDK's documentation. See also cite25†Environment variables and fields for unified authentication and the cite26†Authentication method priority .
L103: 
L104: For cite27†account-level operations , set the following environment variables:
L105:   * `DATABRICKS_HOST`, set to the value of your Databricks account console URL, `https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com`.
L106:   * `DATABRICKS_ACCOUNT_ID`
L107:   * `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID`
L108:   * `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`
L109: 
L110: For cite28†workspace-level operations , set the following environment variables:
L111: 
L112:   * `DATABRICKS_HOST`, set to the value of your Databricks cite24†workspace URL , for example `https://dbc-a1b2345c-d6e7.cloud.databricks.com`.
L113:   * `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID`
L114:   * `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`
L115: Create or identify a Databricks cite29†configuration profile with the following fields in your `.databrickscfg` file. If you create the profile, replace the placeholders with the appropriate values. To use the profile with a tool or SDK, see cite3†Authorize access to Databricks resources or the tool's or SDK's documentation. See also cite25†Environment variables and fields for unified authentication and the cite26†Authentication method priority .
L116: For cite27†account-level operations , set the following values in your `.databrickscfg` file. In this case, the Databricks account console URL is `https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com`:
L117: 
L118:     `[<some-unique-configuration-profile-name>]
L119:     host          = <account-console-url>
L120:     account_id    = <account-id>
L121:     client_id     = <service-principal-client-id>
L122:     client_secret = <service-principal-secret>
L123:     `
L124: For cite28†workspace-level operations , set the following values in your `.databrickscfg` file. In this case, the host is the Databricks cite24†workspace URL , for example `https://dbc-a1b2345c-d6e7.cloud.databricks.com`:
L125: 
L126:     `[<some-unique-configuration-profile-name>]
L127:     host          = <workspace-url>
L128:     client_id     = <service-principal-client-id>
L129:     client_secret = <service-principal-secret>
L130:     `
L131: 
L132: For the Databricks CLI, do one of the following:
L133:   * Set the environment variables as specified on the Environment tab.
L134:   * Set the values in your `.databrickscfg` file as specified on the Profile tab.
L135: 
L136: Environment variables always take precedence over values in your `.databrickscfg` file.
L137: 
L138: See also cite30†OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication .
L139: 
L140: note
L141: 
L142: OAuth service principal authentication is supported on the following Databricks Connect versions:
L143:   * For Python, Databricks Connect for Databricks Runtime 13.1 and above.
L144:   * For Scala, Databricks Connect for Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above.
L145: 
L146: For Databricks Connect, you can either:
L147:   * Use a config profile: Set workspace-level values in your `.databrickscfg` file as described on the Profile tab. Also set the `cluster_id` to your workspace instance URL.
L148:   * Use environment variables: Set the same values as shown on the Environment tab. Also set the `DATABRICKS_CLUSTER_ID` to your workspace instance URL.
L149: 
L150: Values in `.databrickscfg` take precedence over environment variables.
L151: 
L152: To initialize Databricks Connect with these settings, see cite31†Compute configuration for Databricks Connect .
L153: For the Databricks IDE extension, do the following:
L154:   1. Set the values in your `.databrickscfg` file for Databricks cite28†workspace-level operations as specified on the Profile tab.
L155:   2. In the Configuration pane of the Databricks IDE extension, click Configure Databricks.
L156:   3. In the Command Palette, for Databricks Host, enter your cite24†workspace URL , for example `https://dbc-a1b2345c-d6e7.cloud.databricks.com`, and then press `Enter`.
L157:   4. In the Command Palette, select your target profile's name in the list for your URL.
L158: For more details, see cite32†Set up authorization for the Databricks IDE extension .
L159: #### Account-level operationscite33†​ L160: 
L161: For default authentication:
L162: 
L163:     `provider "databricks" {
L164:       alias = "accounts"
L165:     }
L166:     `
L167: 
L168: For direct configuration:
L169: 
L170:     `provider "databricks" {
L171:       alias         = "accounts"
L172:       host          = <retrieve-account-console-url>
L173:       account_id    = <retrieve-account-id>
L174:       client_id     = <retrieve-client-id>
L175:       client_secret = <retrieve-client-secret>
L176:     }
L177:     `
L178: Replace the `retrieve` placeholders with your own implementation to retrieve the values from the console or some other configuration store, such as cite34†HashiCorp Vault†developer.hashicorp.com . See also cite35†Vault Provider†registry.terraform.io . In this case, the Databricks account console URL is `https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com`.
L179: #### Workspace-level operationscite36†​ L180: 
L181: For default configuration:
L182: 
L183:     `provider "databricks" {
L184:       alias = "workspace"
L185:     }
L186:     `
L187: 
L188: For direct configuration:
L189: 
L190:     `provider "databricks" {
L191:       alias         = "workspace"
L192:       host          = <retrieve-workspace-url>
L193:       client_id     = <retrieve-client-id>
L194:       client_secret = <retrieve-client-secret>
L195:     }
L196:     `
L197: Replace the `retrieve` placeholders with your own implementation to retrieve the values from the console or some other configuration store, such as cite34†HashiCorp Vault†developer.hashicorp.com . See also cite35†Vault Provider†registry.terraform.io . In this case, the host is the Databricks cite24†workspace URL , for example `https://dbc-a1b2345c-d6e7.cloud.databricks.com`.
L198: 
L199: For more information about authenticating with the Databricks Terraform provider, see cite37†Authentication†registry.terraform.io .
L200: #### Account-level operationscite38†​ L201: 
L202: For default configuration:
L203: 
L204: Python
L205: 
L206:     `from databricks.sdk import AccountClient
L207:     a = AccountClient()
L208:     # ...
L209:     `
L210: 
L211: For direct configuration:
L212: 
L213: Python
L214: 
L215:     `from databricks.sdk import AccountClient

L217:       host          = retrieve_account_console_url(),
L218:       account_id    = retrieve_account_id(),
L219:       client_id     = retrieve_client_id(),
L220:       client_secret = retrieve_client_secret()

L8: # Connect to serverless compute
L9: 
L10: This page explains how to connect to and use serverless compute for notebooks, workflows, and Lakeflow pipelines in Databricks.
L11: ## What is serverless compute?cite2†​ L12: 
L13: Serverless compute is a Databricks-managed service that allows users to quickly connect to on-demand computing resources for notebooks, workflows, and Lakeflow pipelines.
L14: When you choose to use serverless compute, you can run workloads without provisioning any compute resources in your cloud account. Instead, Databricks automatically allocates and manages the necessary compute resources. This speeds up start-up and scaling times, minimizes idle time, and reduces the need to manage compute resources.
L15: Serverless workloads are protected by multiple layers of security and are designed to be enterprise-ready. For more information, see cite3†Databricks serverless security†www.databricks.com .
L16: 
L17: note
L18: 
L19: Serverless compute is available by default in most workspaces and does not require enablement. Workspaces that have Unity Catalog enabled automatically have access to serverless compute.
L20: Other Databricks features, such as serverless SQL warehouses, model serving, and AI features, use serverless infrastructure independently and have their own configuration paths. This page covers serverless compute for notebooks, workflows, and Lakeflow pipelines only.
L21: ## Use serverless compute for your workloadscite4†​ L22: 
L23: Use the following pages to learn how to configure workloads to use serverless compute:
L24: 
L25:   * cite5†Serverless notebooks L26:   * cite6†Git Folder Serverless (Beta)
L27:   * cite7†Serverless jobs L28:   * cite8†Serverless Lakeflow pipelines L29:   * cite9†Streaming on serverless compute L30: 
L31:   * cite10†AI Runtime (Preview)
L32:   * cite11†Guides for AI Runtime L33: ## Other features that use serverless infrastructurecite12†​ L34: 
L35: Many Databricks features run on serverless infrastructure but are configured and managed separately from serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and Lakeflow pipelines. For example:
L36: 
L37:   * cite13†Serverless SQL warehouses L38:   * cite14†Databricks Model Training - forecasting L39:   * cite15†Data quality monitoring L40:   * cite16†Predictive optimization L41: ## Serverless compute requirementscite17†​ L42: 
L43: Serverless compute is available by default in most workspaces. No manual enablement steps are required.
L44: 
L45: Legacy workspaces that are not enabled for Unity Catalog do not have access to serverless compute. To access serverless compute, you must upgrade to Unity Catalog. See cite18†Upgrade a Databricks workspace to Unity Catalog .
L46: 
L47: ## Serverless compute limitationscite19†​ L48: 
L49: For a list of limitations, see cite20†Serverless compute limitations .
L50: ## Frequently asked questions (FAQ)cite21†​ L51:   * cite22†How are releases rolled out? L52:   * cite23†How do I determine which serverless version I am running? L53:   * cite24†How do I estimate costs for serverless? L54:   * cite25†How do I analyze DBU usage for a specific workload? L55:   * cite26†Is there a delay between when you run a job or query and the appearance of charges on the billable usage system table? L56:   * cite27†Why do I see billing records for serverless jobs even though I haven't run serverless workloads? L57:   * cite28†Does serverless compute support private repos? L58:   * cite29†How do I install libraries for my job tasks? L59:   * cite30†Can I connect to custom data sources? L60:   * cite31†How does the serverless compute plane networking work? L61:   * cite32†Can I configure serverless compute for jobs with Declarative Automation Bundles? L62:   * cite33†How do I run my serverless workload from my local development machine or from my data application? L63: ### How are releases rolled out?cite22†​ L64: 
L65: Serverless compute is a versionless product, which means that Databricks automatically upgrades the serverless compute runtime to support enhancements and upgrades to the platform. All users get the same updates, rolled out over a short period of time.
L66: 
L67: ### How do I determine which serverless version I am running?cite23†​ L68: 
L69: Serverless workloads always run on the latest runtime version. See cite34†Release notes for the most recent version.
L70: ### How do I estimate costs for serverless?cite24†​ L71: 
L72: Databricks recommends running and benchmarking a representative or specific workload and then analyzing the billing system table. See cite35†Billable usage system table reference .
L73: 
L74: ### How do I analyze DBU usage for a specific workload?cite25†​ L75: 
L76: To see the cost for a specific workload, query the `system.billing.usage` system table. See cite36†Monitor the cost of serverless compute for sample queries and to download our cost observability dashboard.
L77: ### Is there a delay between when you run a job or query and the appearance of charges on the billable usage system table?cite26†​ L78: 
L79: Yes, there could be up to a 24-hour delay between when you run a workload and its usage being reflected in the billable usage system table.
L80: ### Why do I see billing records for serverless jobs even though I haven't run serverless workloads?cite27†​ L81: 
L82: cite15†Data quality monitoring and cite16†predictive optimization run on serverless infrastructure and are billed under the serverless jobs SKU. These features are managed separately from serverless compute for notebooks, workflows, and Lakeflow pipelines.
L83: ### Does serverless compute support private repos?cite28†​ L84: 
L85: Repositories can be private or require authentication. For security reasons, a pre-signed URL is required when accessing authenticated repositories.
L86: 
L87: ### How do I install libraries for my job tasks?cite29†​ L88: 
L89: Databricks recommends using environments to install and manage libraries for your jobs. See cite37†Configure environment for job tasks .
L90: ### Can I connect to custom data sources?cite30†​ L91: 
L92: No, only sources that use Lakehouse Federation are supported. See cite38†Supported data sources .
L93: 
L94: ### How does the serverless compute plane networking work?cite31†​ L95: 
L96: Serverless compute resources run in the serverless compute plane, which is managed by Databricks. For more details on the network and architecture, see cite39†Serverless compute plane networking .
L97: ### Can I configure serverless compute for jobs with Declarative Automation Bundles?cite32†​ L98: 
L99: Yes, Declarative Automation Bundles can be used to configure jobs that use serverless compute. See cite40†Job that uses serverless compute .
L100: ### How do I run my serverless workload from my local development machine or from my data application?cite33†​ L101: 
L102: Databricks Connect allows you to connect to Databricks from your local machine and run workloads on serverless. See cite41†Databricks Connect .
